subject: Immunology
stem: A cell degrades cytosolic proteins normally but cannot efficiently move resulting peptides into the ER for class I loading. Which transporter is defective?

options.explanation: CD28 provides T-cell costimulation rather than ER peptide transport.
This complement enzyme does not transport peptides across the ER membrane.
TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the ER for class I loading.
Invariant chain guides class II trafficking rather than importing these peptides.

explanation: Proteasomal peptides must reach the ER to bind newly assembled class I molecules. TAP performs ATP-dependent transport across the ER membrane. Defective transport reduces stable peptide-loaded class I display despite preserved production of peptide fragments in the cytosol.
objective: Identify TAP-dependent ER entry as a distinct class I processing step.
keyPoints: Identify TAP-dependent ER entry as a distinct class I processing step.

subject: Immunology
stem: New class II molecules in the ER must avoid binding available ER peptides before reaching endosomes. Which associated protein initially occupies and protects their groove?

options.explanation: C9 forms complement pores rather than blocking a class II groove.
Invariant chain blocks premature loading and directs class II molecules toward endosomes.
This is associated with class I rather than the class II invariant-chain role.
Perforin participates in cytotoxic killing rather than class II trafficking.

explanation: Invariant chain associates with newly synthesized class II molecules, protecting their peptide-binding groove and directing endosomal trafficking. Proteolysis leaves CLIP in the groove until peptide exchange occurs. This compartmentalization favors loading of peptides derived from endosomal proteins.
objective: Explain invariant-chain prevention of premature class II peptide loading.
keyPoints: Explain invariant-chain prevention of premature class II peptide loading.

subject: Immunology
stem: An antigen-presenting cell reaches an acidic endosomal compartment but retains CLIP in class II grooves. Which molecule normally facilitates CLIP release and peptide exchange?

options.explanation: HLA-DM promotes exchange of CLIP for suitable antigenic peptides.
TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the ER for class I loading.
CD8 is a class I-associated T-cell coreceptor rather than this editing molecule.
IgE binds mast-cell receptors and does not catalyze class II peptide exchange.

explanation: Invariant-chain degradation leaves CLIP bound to class II. HLA-DM assists removal and exchange for endosomal peptides, helping select stable complexes for surface display. A failure at this step differs from absent antigen uptake or failure to transport cytosolic peptides through TAP.
objective: Identify HLA-DM-mediated CLIP exchange in class II processing.
keyPoints: Identify HLA-DM-mediated CLIP exchange in class II processing.

subject: Immunology
stem: A dendritic cell takes up material from an infected dying cell and activates naive CD8 T cells without itself being infected. Which presentation process explains this?

options.text: Presentation on class II to CD8 alone
options.explanation: Conventional CD8 recognition is associated with class I rather than class II.

options.text: Antibody gene transfer into the T cell
options.explanation: T-cell priming does not require acquisition of antibody genes.

options.text: Direct infection of every responding T cell
options.explanation: The described priming can occur without infecting the T cells.

options.text: Cross-presentation of exogenous antigen on class I
options.explanation: Dendritic cells can route acquired extracellular antigens into class I presentation.

explanation: Some dendritic cells can present acquired extracellular material on class I molecules. This cross-presentation allows CD8 priming against infected tissues that do not directly infect the presenting cell. It bridges antigen acquisition and cytotoxic T-cell activation without changing coreceptor specificity.
objective: Integrate extracellular antigen uptake with class I-dependent CD8 priming.

subject: Immunology
stem: A naive T cell recognizes peptide-MHC on an antigen-presenting cell lacking B7 molecules. Which missing interaction normally supports full activation?

options.explanation: IgE-mediated red-cell binding does not provide the required naive T-cell signal.

options.text: Intrinsic factor binding to class I
options.explanation: Intrinsic factor is a digestive binding protein rather than a costimulatory ligand.
B7 ligands provide a major costimulatory signal through T-cell CD28.
This interaction is not a physiologic T-cell costimulation mechanism.

explanation: Naive T-cell activation normally requires antigen-receptor recognition plus costimulation. B7 molecules on activated antigen-presenting cells bind CD28 and support survival and proliferation. Antigen recognition without adequate costimulation can favor nonresponsiveness rather than a complete productive response.
objective: Identify B7-CD28 as a major naive T-cell costimulatory interaction.
keyPoints: Identify B7-CD28 as a major naive T-cell costimulatory interaction.

subject: Immunology
stem: An activated T cell increases expression of a receptor that binds B7 and limits subsequent activation. Which receptor provides this inhibitory checkpoint?

options.explanation: CD19 is a B-cell coreceptor component rather than this T-cell checkpoint.
CTLA-4 binds B7 and restrains T-cell activation.
CD28 primarily provides positive rather than inhibitory costimulation.
CD3 transduces antigen-receptor signals rather than serving as the B7 inhibitory receptor.

explanation: Activated T cells increase CTLA-4 expression as part of feedback restraint. CTLA-4 engages B7 and limits activation, in contrast with the positive signal supplied through CD28. Similar ligand recognition can therefore lead to different effects depending on the T-cell receptor involved.
objective: Distinguish CTLA-4 restraint from CD28 costimulation.
keyPoints: Distinguish CTLA-4 restraint from CD28 costimulation.

subject: Immunology
stem: Developing thymocytes fail to recognize any self-MHC molecule with sufficient affinity. Which developmental outcome is most likely in normal positive selection?

options.explanation: Cells without usable self-MHC recognition fail to receive survival signals.

options.text: Automatic differentiation into every effector lineage
options.explanation: A usable receptor signal is needed before normal T-cell maturation.
Thymocytes are not antibody-producing B cells.

options.text: Preferential survival solely because recognition is absent
options.explanation: Absent recognition fails the positive-selection requirement.

explanation: Positive selection preserves thymocytes whose receptors can recognize self-MHC sufficiently to receive survival signals. Cells lacking usable recognition undergo death by neglect. This is different from negative selection, which removes many cells with excessively strong self-reactivity.
objective: Explain loss of thymocytes that cannot recognize self-MHC during positive selection.
keyPoints: Explain loss of thymocytes that cannot recognize self-MHC during positive selection.

subject: Immunology
stem: A thymic epithelial defect reduces expression of proteins normally restricted to peripheral tissues. Which tolerance process is most directly weakened?

options.explanation: Thymic epithelial proteins do not produce bacterial capsules.

options.text: Transport of IgA through intestinal epithelium
options.explanation: Mucosal antibody transport is not the thymic antigen-display function.

options.text: Class I peptide movement through TAP
options.explanation: Tissue-antigen transcription is distinct from the ER transporter itself.

options.text: Deletion of strongly self-reactive developing T cells
options.explanation: Tissue-antigen display helps eliminate thymocytes that could attack peripheral tissues.

explanation: AIRE promotes expression of many tissue-restricted antigens in medullary thymic epithelial cells. Their display supports central tolerance by exposing developing T cells to peripheral self components. Reduced display can permit escape of autoreactive clones despite an anatomically present thymus.
objective: Connect AIRE-dependent tissue antigen display to central T-cell tolerance.
keyPoints: Connect AIRE-dependent tissue antigen display to central T-cell tolerance.

subject: Immunology
stem: An immature marrow B cell strongly recognizes self antigen and resumes light-chain gene rearrangement. What tolerance mechanism is this cell attempting?

options.text: Somatic mutation of every T-cell receptor
options.explanation: The described cell is a B cell altering its light-chain rearrangement.
Complement lysis does not repair a self-reactive antigen receptor.
New light-chain rearrangement can change specificity away from the self antigen.
Changing the constant region does not ordinarily change antigen-binding specificity.

explanation: Immature self-reactive B cells can reactivate light-chain rearrangement to produce a different receptor. Successful editing may remove self-reactivity and permit survival. This changes antigen-binding specificity and differs from class switching, which mainly changes antibody effector function.
objective: Explain light-chain receptor editing as a central B-cell tolerance mechanism.
keyPoints: Explain light-chain receptor editing as a central B-cell tolerance mechanism.

subject: Immunology
stem: After repeated exposure to one protein antigen, antibodies bind it more tightly even when compared within the same isotype. Which process explains the increased affinity?

options.text: Loss of every antigen-specific B cell
options.explanation: Eliminating all specific clones would not improve antigen-specific affinity.

options.text: Selection of somatically mutated variable regions
options.explanation: Germinal-center mutation and selection enrich higher-affinity B-cell clones.

options.text: Constant-region switching as the sole explanation
options.explanation: Switching isotype changes effector function rather than directly increasing binding affinity.

options.text: Replacement of all antibodies by complement
options.explanation: Complement does not become the antigen-binding variable region.

explanation: Activated B cells undergo somatic hypermutation in immunoglobulin variable-region genes. Competition for antigen and T-cell help selects clones with improved binding. This affinity maturation can occur alongside class switching, but the two processes change different antibody properties.
objective: Separate variable-region affinity maturation from constant-region class switching.
keyPoints: Separate variable-region affinity maturation from constant-region class switching.

subject: Immunology
stem: Two blood samples follow first and later exposure to the same antigen. The later response is faster and includes higher-affinity IgG. Which cellular population best explains this?

options.explanation: Memory cells respond rapidly and can generate affinity-matured antibody output.
Red cells do not provide antigen-specific immunoglobulin memory.
Neutrophils lack the clonally rearranged antibody memory system.
These are not the source of the observed B-cell antibody memory.

explanation: Primary responses establish memory B cells after antigen-driven expansion and selection. On re-exposure, these cells respond more rapidly and can produce class-switched, higher-affinity antibodies. The combination of timing and affinity distinguishes memory from simply increasing nonspecific inflammatory cells.
objective: Integrate response speed and antibody affinity as evidence of B-cell memory.
keyPoints: Integrate response speed and antibody affinity as evidence of B-cell memory.

subject: Immunology
stem: A dimeric antibody made beneath intestinal epithelium enters the lumen with a secretory component attached. Which receptor mediates its epithelial transcytosis?

options.text: Neonatal Fc receptor as the IgA-specific route
options.explanation: FcRn chiefly handles IgG and is not the principal polymeric IgA transporter.
CD28 mediates T-cell costimulation rather than epithelial antibody export.
TAP transports peptides across the ER membrane rather than intact IgA.
This receptor transports polymeric IgA across mucosal epithelium.

explanation: Dimeric IgA containing a J chain binds the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor basolaterally. Transcytosis and receptor cleavage release secretory IgA into the lumen with a protective secretory component. Mucosal antibody production and epithelial delivery are therefore distinct steps.
objective: Identify polymeric immunoglobulin receptor transport of secretory IgA.
keyPoints: Identify polymeric immunoglobulin receptor transport of secretory IgA.

subject: Immunology
stem: Maternal antibody crosses the placenta and provides temporary systemic protection to a newborn. Which antibody class is preferentially transferred through Fc receptor-mediated transport?

options.explanation: IgE is not the principal antibody class transferred for systemic neonatal protection.
Secretory IgA principally supports mucosal protection rather than placental systemic transfer.
Placental FcRn-mediated transport preferentially transfers maternal IgG.
The large pentameric IgM molecule is not normally transferred efficiently across placenta.

explanation: Maternal IgG is transported across the placenta through Fc receptor-dependent pathways, providing passive systemic immunity. The infant did not generate this antibody through its own antigen response. This protection wanes as maternal IgG is cleared after birth.
objective: Identify IgG as the major placentally transferred antibody class.
keyPoints: Identify IgG as the major placentally transferred antibody class.

subject: Immunology
stem: Antigen-bound IgM exposes complement-binding sites and initiates the classical pathway. Which complement component first recognizes the antibody Fc arrangement?

options.explanation: This recognizes microbial carbohydrates in the lectin rather than antibody classical pathway.
C1q binds appropriately arranged Fc regions in antigen-antibody complexes.
C9 acts at the terminal membrane attack stage rather than initial recognition.
Factor D functions in alternative-pathway convertase formation.

explanation: C1q recognizes Fc regions arranged by antigen-bound antibody, activating associated C1 proteases and the classical cascade. Subsequent steps generate convertases and effector fragments. Initial antibody recognition therefore differs from alternative-pathway amplification and terminal pore formation.
objective: Identify C1q as the recognition component of antibody-initiated complement.
keyPoints: Identify C1q as the recognition component of antibody-initiated complement.

subject: Immunology
stem: Bacteria coated with a complement fragment are engulfed more efficiently through phagocyte complement receptors. Which fragment principally provides this opsonizing signal?

options.explanation: Surface-bound C3b tags particles for recognition by complement receptors.
C3a is a soluble inflammatory mediator rather than the principal surface opsonin.
C5a strongly recruits and activates leukocytes rather than acting as the principal surface coat.
C9 participates in pores rather than serving as the main phagocytic coat.

explanation: C3 activation exposes reactive groups that permit C3b attachment to microbial surfaces. Phagocytes recognize bound complement through specific receptors, improving uptake. Soluble C3a and C5a instead promote inflammatory signaling, separating opsonization from recruitment and permeability effects.
objective: Distinguish surface C3b opsonization from soluble complement inflammatory fragments.
keyPoints: Distinguish surface C3b opsonization from soluble complement inflammatory fragments.

subject: Immunology
stem: A bacterial focus generates a complement-derived gradient that strongly recruits neutrophils. Which soluble fragment is a particularly potent chemoattractant?

options.explanation: C1q primarily recognizes initiating complexes rather than serving as this major gradient.
C9 is a membrane attack complex component rather than a dominant soluble chemoattractant.
Intact C4 is not the potent neutrophil chemoattractant described.
C5a recruits and activates neutrophils through specific surface receptors.

explanation: Complement activation produces C5a, a powerful inflammatory and chemotactic signal. Neutrophils sense gradients through receptors and migrate toward the source. This recruitment function is distinct from C3b-mediated surface tagging and C5b-9 pore formation.
objective: Identify C5a as a potent complement-derived neutrophil chemoattractant.
keyPoints: Identify C5a as a potent complement-derived neutrophil chemoattractant.

subject: Immunology
stem: A normal host cell expresses a membrane protein that accelerates dissociation of complement convertases. Which protective protein performs this decay-accelerating role?

options.explanation: CD3 transduces T-cell receptor signals rather than restraining surface convertases.
CD19 participates in B-cell signaling rather than serving as decay-accelerating factor.
CD55 limits complement activation by accelerating convertase decay.
CD28 supports T-cell costimulation rather than complement convertase decay.

explanation: Host membranes display complement regulatory proteins to limit collateral injury. CD55, also called decay-accelerating factor, destabilizes convertases. Its function differs from CD59, which inhibits terminal membrane attack assembly, although both help protect host cells.
objective: Identify CD55-mediated acceleration of complement convertase decay.
keyPoints: Identify CD55-mediated acceleration of complement convertase decay.

subject: Immunology
stem: A virally infected cell reduces surface class I expression to evade cytotoxic T cells. Which innate lymphocyte can detect the resulting loss of inhibitory self signals?

options.explanation: Eosinophils do not provide the canonical class I missing-self pathway.
Reduced self class I can remove inhibitory NK receptor signaling.
Red cells are not cytotoxic lymphocytes with missing-self recognition.
Plasma cells secrete antibodies rather than perform this innate cytotoxic sensing.

explanation: NK cells integrate activating signals with inhibition supplied by self class I recognition. Loss of class I can reduce inhibition and permit killing when activating cues are sufficient. This provides a countermeasure against pathogens or tumors that evade class I-dependent T-cell recognition.
objective: Explain NK surveillance of cells with reduced self class I display.
keyPoints: Explain NK surveillance of cells with reduced self class I display.

subject: Immunology
stem: An antibody coats a tumor cell and an NK cell binds its Fc region before releasing cytotoxic granules. Which NK receptor commonly mediates this antibody-dependent recognition?

options.explanation: CD16 binds IgG Fc and supports antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
CD4 is a class II-associated T-cell coreceptor rather than the NK IgG Fc receptor.
CD8 binds class I and does not perform the described IgG Fc recognition.
TAP is an intracellular peptide transporter rather than a surface Fc receptor.

explanation: NK cells express CD16, an Fc receptor that recognizes IgG coating a target. Cross-linking activates cytotoxic granule release and target killing. Antibody provides specificity while the NK cell supplies the effector mechanism, distinguishing ADCC from direct complement-mediated lysis.
objective: Identify CD16-mediated NK recognition during antibody-dependent cytotoxicity.
keyPoints: Identify CD16-mediated NK recognition during antibody-dependent cytotoxicity.

subject: Immunology
stem: A cytotoxic lymphocyte releases granules at a target-cell contact. Which granule enzyme enters the target and activates pathways leading to apoptosis?

options.explanation: Catalase disposes of peroxide rather than acting as the principal cytotoxic granule protease.
Amylase digests carbohydrate and does not trigger the described target-cell apoptosis.
Telomerase maintains chromosome ends rather than acting as a secreted cytotoxic protease.
Granzymes enter target cells and initiate proteolytic apoptotic pathways.

explanation: Cytotoxic lymphocytes release perforin and granzymes into a specialized contact. Perforin supports granzyme access to the target, where granzymes activate apoptotic pathways. Target death is therefore an organized intracellular response rather than simply indiscriminate extracellular digestion.
objective: Distinguish granzyme apoptotic signaling from noncytotoxic enzyme functions.
keyPoints: Distinguish granzyme apoptotic signaling from noncytotoxic enzyme functions.

subject: Immunology
stem: After an immune response, an activated T cell receives a Fas ligand signal that recruits a death-inducing complex. Which upstream apoptosis route is engaged?

options.explanation: Fas-mediated apoptosis does not require a terminal complement pore.
Changing an immunoglobulin constant region does not initiate this T-cell death pathway.
Fas recruits adaptor and initiator caspase machinery at a surface death receptor.
Fas signaling begins at a membrane death receptor rather than nutrient withdrawal.

explanation: Fas is a death receptor that assembles an intracellular signaling complex after ligand binding. Initiator caspases activate downstream apoptotic machinery, helping remove activated lymphocytes. This receptor-triggered route is distinct from initiating apoptosis through mitochondrial growth-factor withdrawal.
objective: Identify Fas-mediated initiation of extrinsic lymphocyte apoptosis.
keyPoints: Identify Fas-mediated initiation of extrinsic lymphocyte apoptosis.

subject: Immunology
stem: A recently activated T cell produces a cytokine and increases high-affinity receptors for it, promoting its own clonal proliferation. Which cytokine best fits this autocrine loop?

options.explanation: Calcitonin is not the principal cytokine driving activated T-cell clonal expansion.
IL-2 supports expansion of activated T cells and also regulatory T-cell maintenance.
Erythropoietin primarily stimulates erythroid production rather than this T-cell loop.
Thyroxine is an endocrine metabolic hormone rather than the autocrine cytokine described.

explanation: Antigen recognition and costimulation induce IL-2 production and high-affinity IL-2 receptor expression. The cytokine then supports proliferation of responsive lymphocytes through autocrine and paracrine signaling. This expansion follows activation rather than replacing the antigen recognition requirement.
objective: Explain the IL-2 growth loop following productive T-cell activation.
keyPoints: Explain the IL-2 growth loop following productive T-cell activation.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Immunology
stem: An antigen-presenting cell releases a cytokine that favors differentiation of naive helper T cells toward interferon-gamma-producing effectors. Which cytokine is most characteristic?

options.explanation: IL-12 promotes Th1 differentiation and supports interferon-gamma responses.
IL-4 instead favors Th2 differentiation in the usual polarization framework.
This hormone supports erythroid cells rather than helper T-cell polarization.
Insulin is not the antigen-presenting-cell cytokine driving Th1 differentiation.

explanation: IL-12 from activated antigen-presenting cells promotes a Th1 program in responding helper T cells. These cells produce interferon-gamma and support responses against intracellular pathogens. The question concerns differentiation signals rather than the downstream macrophage-activating action of interferon-gamma.
objective: Identify IL-12 as an upstream driver of Th1 polarization.
keyPoints: Identify IL-12 as an upstream driver of Th1 polarization.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Immunology
stem: A naive helper T cell differentiates in an IL-4-rich environment and subsequently supports eosinophilic and IgE-associated responses. Which transcriptional helper program is favored?

options.text: Th1 differentiation as the dominant direct effect
options.explanation: IL-12 and interferon-gamma rather than IL-4 favor the classic Th1 program.
Helper T-cell polarization does not transform the cell into an erythrocyte.
Polarization alters effector function without abolishing antigen receptor specificity.
IL-4 promotes the Th2 program associated with type 2 immune responses.

explanation: IL-4 supports differentiation toward Th2 cells, which produce cytokines participating in type 2 responses. These responses can support parasite defense and allergic inflammation. Polarization determines effector behavior while the rearranged antigen receptor retains its recognition specificity.
objective: Connect IL-4 exposure with helper T-cell type 2 differentiation.
keyPoints: Connect IL-4 exposure with helper T-cell type 2 differentiation.

subject: Immunology
stem: A mucosal T-cell response induces epithelial chemokines that recruit neutrophils against extracellular organisms. Which helper-cell cytokine is particularly associated with this response?

options.explanation: Erythropoietin supports erythropoiesis rather than barrier neutrophil recruitment.
Melatonin conveys circadian information rather than the specific helper-cell effector signal.
IL-17 promotes tissue chemokine and growth-factor responses supporting neutrophils.
IL-4 chiefly supports type 2 differentiation rather than this neutrophil program.

explanation: Th17-associated IL-17 acts on epithelial and stromal cells to stimulate mediators supporting neutrophil recruitment and production. This helps defend barriers against selected extracellular bacteria and fungi. It differs from direct antibody neutralization or Th2-driven eosinophilic responses.
objective: Associate IL-17 with barrier-driven neutrophil recruitment.
keyPoints: Associate IL-17 with barrier-driven neutrophil recruitment.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Immunology
stem: A lymphocyte population expresses CD4, high CD25, and the transcription factor FOXP3 and restrains immune activation. Which lineage is most characteristic?

options.explanation: NK cells use a different developmental and recognition program.
FOXP3 is a defining regulator of the canonical regulatory T-cell program.
Plasma cells specialize in antibody secretion rather than the FOXP3 program.
Neutrophils do not comprise this CD4-positive regulatory lymphocyte lineage.

explanation: FOXP3 supports the development and suppressive functions of canonical regulatory T cells. These cells help maintain peripheral tolerance and constrain excessive responses. High CD25 expression supports IL-2 responsiveness but should be interpreted with the complete phenotype rather than alone.
objective: Identify the FOXP3-associated regulatory T-cell lineage.
keyPoints: Identify the FOXP3-associated regulatory T-cell lineage.

subject: Immunology
stem: A macrophage exposed to a regulatory cytokine decreases production of several inflammatory mediators and its ability to stimulate T cells. Which cytokine best fits?

options.explanation: IL-10 restrains many macrophage and antigen-presenting-cell inflammatory functions.
Interferon-gamma generally enhances classical macrophage activation.
IL-12 supports type 1 responses rather than this principal suppressive effect.
G-CSF principally supports granulocyte production rather than defining this suppression.

explanation: IL-10 acts on macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells to limit inflammatory cytokine output and stimulatory activity. This helps regulate immune response intensity. The effect contrasts with interferon-gamma-driven activation and does not imply elimination of every host defense function.
objective: Explain IL-10-mediated restraint of inflammatory antigen-presenting cells.
keyPoints: Explain IL-10-mediated restraint of inflammatory antigen-presenting cells.

subject: Immunology
stem: A bacterial protein causes broad T-cell activation without conventional peptide processing and binds outside the usual peptide-specific recognition site. Which mechanism explains this?

options.text: Precise binding to one unique processed peptide clone
options.explanation: The broad response is not limited to one conventional peptide-specific clone.

options.text: Destruction of every T-cell receptor gene
options.explanation: The acute response requires receptor engagement rather than deletion of all receptor genes.

options.text: Direct neutralization of all inflammatory cytokines
options.explanation: The protein causes activation rather than cytokine neutralization.

options.text: Crosslinking class II and selected TCR V-beta regions
options.explanation: Superantigens activate many T cells sharing susceptible V-beta families.

explanation: Superantigens bind class II molecules and T-cell receptor V-beta regions outside ordinary peptide-specific contacts. This recruits a much broader T-cell population than conventional antigen presentation and can cause intense cytokine release. Lack of usual processing and broad activation identify the mechanism together.
objective: Integrate processing independence and broad T-cell activation to identify superantigen action.
keyPoints: Integrate processing independence and broad T-cell activation to identify superantigen action.

subject: Immunology
stem: A highly repetitive bacterial polysaccharide activates B cells without conventional protein-specific T-cell help. Which property helps produce this T-independent response?

options.text: Direct conversion of B cells into helper T cells
options.explanation: T-independent activation does not require lineage conversion.

options.text: Elimination of all innate accessory signals
options.explanation: T-independent responses can still depend on innate signals and cellular context.
Repeated epitopes engage multiple receptors and can strongly stimulate appropriate B cells.

options.text: Presentation of polysaccharide peptides on class II
options.explanation: Pure polysaccharide does not become a conventional peptide antigen by this route.

explanation: Repetitive polysaccharide arrays can crosslink many B-cell receptors and activate selected B-cell populations with limited conventional T-cell help. These responses generally have less robust memory and affinity maturation than protein-linked responses. T-independent does not mean independent of every accessory signal.
objective: Explain B-cell receptor crosslinking by repetitive T-independent polysaccharides.
keyPoints: Explain B-cell receptor crosslinking by repetitive T-independent polysaccharides.

subject: Immunology
stem: A B cell binds a capsule polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein, internalizes the conjugate, and receives carrier-specific T-cell help. Why does linkage improve the response?

options.text: The conjugate removes the need for antigen-specific B cells
options.explanation: Specific B-cell capture remains central to the linked response.

options.text: The B cell presents carrier peptides after capturing its target polysaccharide
options.explanation: Linked recognition supplies T-cell help to the polysaccharide-specific B cell.

options.text: The carrier turns polysaccharide into a peptide chemically
options.explanation: The carbohydrate remains carbohydrate; carrier protein provides presentable peptides.

options.text: All T cells directly recognize free polysaccharide on class I
options.explanation: Conventional helper recognition uses carrier peptides with class II.

explanation: A polysaccharide-specific B cell captures the linked conjugate through its receptor and presents carrier-derived peptides on class II. Carrier-specific helper cells can then provide cognate help to that B cell. Physical linkage coordinates antigen capture and peptide presentation, supporting stronger memory and maturation.

subject: Immunology
stem: Early lymphoid cells cannot make the programmed DNA cuts needed to assemble antigen receptor variable regions. Which enzyme complex normally initiates this rearrangement?

options.explanation: RAG proteins recognize recombination signals and initiate V(D)J rearrangement.
Telomerase extends chromosome ends rather than initiating antigen receptor gene assembly.
Catalase detoxifies peroxide rather than rearranging lymphocyte receptor DNA.
Enteropeptidase activates intestinal trypsinogen rather than receptor genes.

explanation: RAG1 and RAG2 recognize recombination signal sequences and initiate breaks for V(D)J recombination. Joining selected variable, diversity, and joining segments generates antigen receptor diversity in developing B and T cells. This occurs before antigen-driven somatic hypermutation of mature B cells.
objective: Identify RAG initiation of antigen receptor V(D)J recombination.
keyPoints: Identify RAG initiation of antigen receptor V(D)J recombination.

subject: Immunology
stem: During antigen receptor assembly, nucleotides not encoded by the adjacent gene segments are added at joining sites. Which enzyme produces this source of diversity?

options.explanation: Helicase unwinds DNA rather than specifically adding non-templated junctional bases.
This enzyme transcribes ribosomal RNA rather than creating receptor joining diversity.
This metabolic enzyme does not catalyze receptor DNA junctional changes.
TdT adds non-templated nucleotides during receptor gene joining.

explanation: TdT adds nucleotides without a DNA template at coding joins during V(D)J recombination. Together with trimming and segment choice, this creates highly diverse antigen-binding regions. Junctional addition is a developmental DNA assembly process rather than later protein glycosylation.
objective: Identify TdT-generated non-templated receptor junctional diversity.

subject: Immunology
stem: A developing B cell successfully rearranges one heavy-chain allele and suppresses productive rearrangement of the second. What is the principal functional result?

options.text: Loss of all population-level antibody diversity
options.explanation: Different clones retain distinct rearrangements across the population.

options.text: Automatic switching to every constant-region isotype
options.explanation: Heavy-chain allelic exclusion is distinct from later isotype switching.

options.text: One dominant antigen receptor specificity per B cell
options.explanation: Allelic exclusion helps maintain coherent clonal receptor specificity.

options.text: Expression of every possible antibody in one cell
options.explanation: The process restricts rather than maximizes receptor diversity within a single cell.

explanation: A successful receptor rearrangement generates feedback limiting additional productive rearrangements. This allelic exclusion supports a single dominant receptor specificity in an individual B-cell clone. Diversity remains extensive across clones, allowing clonal selection while preserving a coherent response within each clone.
objective: Explain allelic exclusion as support for B-cell clonal specificity.
keyPoints: Explain allelic exclusion as support for B-cell clonal specificity.

subject: Genetics
stem: Sequencing finds a rare missense variant, but segregation and functional evidence are insufficient. Which interpretation best reflects a variant of uncertain significance?

options.text: Every missense variant is definitively benign
options.explanation: Missense variants can have diverse functional effects.

options.text: The finding automatically explains all symptoms
options.explanation: Causal attribution requires evidence beyond the mere presence of a variant.

options.text: Available evidence does not establish pathogenicity or benignity
options.explanation: Uncertain classification records limited evidence rather than a confirmed cause.

options.text: Rarity alone proves the disease mechanism
options.explanation: Many rare variants are not disease-causing, so rarity is insufficient.

explanation: A variant of uncertain significance lacks enough evidence for a confident pathogenic or benign classification. Rarity and a plausible gene are insufficient by themselves. Segregation, functional data, population evidence, and other findings may later permit reclassification, but uncertainty must remain explicit meanwhile.
objective: Interpret uncertain variant classification without treating rarity as proof of causality.
keyPoints: Interpret uncertain variant classification without treating rarity as proof of causality.

subject: Genetics
stem: Two pathogenic variants are found in an autosomal recessive gene. Parental testing shows one was inherited from each parent on opposite homologues. What does this establish?

options.text: Every neighboring gene is also deleted
options.explanation: Sequence variants do not establish a contiguous gene deletion.
Opposite homologues can each carry a disrupted allele of the recessive gene.

options.text: Both variants must be on one chromosome
options.explanation: Separate parental homologues indicate trans rather than cis phase.
Biallelic variants are compatible with a recessive mechanism.

explanation: Phase describes whether variants occupy the same homologue or opposite homologues. One variant on each parental chromosome establishes trans configuration and can support biallelic involvement in a recessive disorder. Two variants in cis may instead leave the other allele intact, changing interpretation.
objective: Use parental origin to distinguish trans from cis variants in a recessive gene.
keyPoints: Use parental origin to distinguish trans from cis variants in a recessive gene.

subject: Genetics
stem: Short sequencing reads map equally well to a functional gene and a highly similar inactive copy. An apparent pathogenic call disappears with locus-specific testing. What most likely occurred?

options.explanation: Highly similar sequences can cause reads from one locus to be assigned to another.

options.text: Universal reversion of the variant in every cell
options.explanation: A technical mapping explanation fits the locus-specific discrepancy better.

options.text: A necessary change in the persons parentage
options.explanation: Read mapping error does not imply a biological relationship change.

options.text: Proof that all sequencing is useless
options.explanation: A locus-specific artifact does not invalidate every sequencing method.

explanation: Pseudogenes can share extensive sequence identity with functional genes. Short reads may be assigned incorrectly, creating false variant calls at the functional locus. Locus-specific amplification or other validated methods can distinguish the sequences and resolve the apparent finding.
objective: Infer pseudogene misalignment from homologous reads and locus-specific confirmation.

subject: Genetics
stem: A common marker is associated with a disease because it is often inherited with a nearby causal variant. The marker itself has no demonstrated functional effect. Which explanation fits?

options.text: Association proves direct protein disruption by the marker
options.explanation: A statistical association alone does not establish a functional mechanism.

options.text: Every associated allele must be on a different chromosome
options.explanation: Nearby variants can be inherited together on the same chromosome.

options.text: A marker can never predict anything unless it is causal
options.explanation: Correlated inheritance can produce predictive association without direct causation.

options.text: Linkage disequilibrium with the causal variant
options.explanation: Nonrandom co-inheritance can make a marker associate without being mechanistically causal.

explanation: Nearby variants may occur together more often than expected because of shared inheritance history and limited recombination. A marker can therefore track a causal allele without altering biological function itself. Functional or fine-mapping evidence is needed to distinguish the associated marker from the causal change.
objective: Distinguish linked marker association from direct variant causality.
keyPoints: Distinguish linked marker association from direct variant causality.

subject: Genetics
stem: A child has a heterozygous variant present across tested tissues but absent from both parents routine samples. Which origin is compatible with this apparently de novo finding?

options.text: Only infection of the child with a DNA virus
options.explanation: A constitutional sequence variant need not result from infection.

options.text: Proof that sibling recurrence risk is absolutely zero
options.explanation: Possible parental germline mosaicism prevents that absolute inference.

options.text: A new variant in a parental gamete or very early embryo
options.explanation: An early event can produce a broadly distributed variant absent from parental blood.

options.text: Mandatory inheritance from an affected grandparent
options.explanation: An apparently new variant does not require an affected grandparent.

explanation: A de novo variant may arise in a gamete or early after fertilization and be absent from routine parental samples. Broad tissue distribution supports an early event but does not determine its exact timing. Germline mosaicism remains one reason not to infer an absolute zero recurrence risk.
objective: Identify plausible early origins of an apparently de novo constitutional variant.

subject: Genetics
stem: A pathogenic variant in one extracellular matrix gene affects the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system. Which term describes multiple organ effects from one gene?

options.explanation: The stem describes multiple manifestations rather than absent disease features.
One gene can influence multiple distinct phenotypic traits or organ systems.
That refers to different genes producing a similar phenotype rather than one gene affecting many organs.
Allelic exclusion restricts receptor expression and does not describe multisystem effects.

explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when one gene contributes to several phenotypic traits. A widely used matrix component can affect multiple tissues through shared structural functions. This differs from locus heterogeneity, where different genes converge on a similar phenotype.
objective: Recognize multiple organ effects of a single gene as pleiotropy.

subject: Microbiology
stem: Bacteria acquire a new trait after exposure to purified donor DNA. Adding DNase before exposure prevents transfer, and no phage or cell contact is needed. Which mechanism fits?

options.explanation: Competent bacteria can take up extracellular DNA that is vulnerable to DNase.
Conjugation requires donor-recipient interaction rather than purified naked DNA alone.
Transduction uses a phage carrier rather than unprotected extracellular DNA.

options.text: Spontaneous mutation as the sole mechanism
options.explanation: Dependence on donor DNA and DNase sensitivity support acquisition rather than chance mutation alone.

explanation: Transformation introduces extracellular DNA into a competent bacterium. DNase can destroy exposed donor DNA before uptake, preventing transfer. The absence of required donor contact or a phage carrier distinguishes this process from conjugation and transduction.
objective: Use DNase sensitivity and carrier independence to identify bacterial transformation.
keyPoints: Use DNase sensitivity and carrier independence to identify bacterial transformation.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacteriophage particle accidentally packages random donor bacterial DNA and transfers a metabolic gene to a recipient. Many different loci can be transferred. Which mechanism is shown?

options.explanation: Specialized transfer favors loci adjacent to a particular prophage integration site.
The DNA is carried in a phage particle rather than taken up unprotected.
The experiment does not require direct donor-recipient conjugative contact.
Packaging errors can transfer varied bacterial loci through a phage carrier.

explanation: Generalized transduction results when phage packaging includes bacterial DNA instead of the usual viral genome. Different donor regions can be transferred through such particles. Random locus transfer and a phage carrier together distinguish it from specialized transduction and transformation.
objective: Integrate random locus transfer with phage carriage to identify generalized transduction.
keyPoints: Integrate random locus transfer with phage carriage to identify generalized transduction.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A temperate phage excises incorrectly from a bacterial chromosome and carries a nearby host gene. Only genes adjacent to its insertion site are transferred. What process is this?

options.explanation: The transfer described depends on a phage rather than naked DNA uptake.
Cell division alone does not explain a phage moving a neighboring gene to another cell.
Imprecise prophage excision transfers selected neighboring bacterial genes.
Generalized packaging can transfer many loci without the same insertion-site restriction.

explanation: A prophage occupies a specific chromosomal site. Imprecise excision can include adjacent bacterial DNA, producing a specialized transducing particle. The restricted host gene set reflects the integration position, unlike the broad locus range of generalized transduction.
objective: Infer specialized transduction from prophage excision and neighboring-gene restriction.
keyPoints: Infer specialized transduction from prophage excision and neighboring-gene restriction.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacterium becomes toxigenic only after a temperate phage establishes a prophage carrying the toxin gene. Which term describes this acquired phenotype?

options.explanation: The trait is genetically encoded by a prophage rather than inherited as free toxin.
Expression of a phage-encoded gene changes the bacterial phenotype.
Chromosome segregation failure does not explain the phage-supplied toxin gene.
The bacterium retains its genome and gains expression of an additional phage gene.

explanation: Temperate phages can persist as prophages and encode products that alter bacterial behavior. A toxin encoded by the phage can make the lysogen toxigenic, called lysogenic conversion. This differs from transduction of a donor bacterial gene carried accidentally by the phage.
objective: Distinguish phage-encoded toxin conversion from transfer of donor bacterial genes.
keyPoints: Distinguish phage-encoded toxin conversion from transfer of donor bacterial genes.

subject: Microbiology
stem: Two otherwise matched bacterial strains differ only in capsule production. The encapsulated strain resists uptake by phagocytes before specific opsonizing antibody appears. Why?

options.text: The capsule impedes efficient phagocytic recognition and uptake
options.explanation: Surface polysaccharide can shield targets that would otherwise support engulfment.

options.text: The capsule replaces all bacterial ribosomes
options.explanation: Capsules are surface structures rather than protein-synthesis machinery.
Capsular polysaccharides are not the main bacterial energy-generating organelles.

options.text: Every capsule directly destroys phagocyte DNA
options.explanation: Antiphagocytic shielding does not require direct nuclear DNA destruction.

explanation: Capsules can impede attachment and engulfment by phagocytes. Opsonizing antibodies and complement improve recognition of encapsulated organisms and may overcome this barrier. The experiment isolates a surface defense mechanism rather than a change in bacterial metabolism or a universal toxin action.
objective: Explain capsule-associated resistance to unopsonized phagocytosis.
keyPoints: Explain capsule-associated resistance to unopsonized phagocytosis.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A mucosal bacterium releases a protease that cleaves secretory IgA near its hinge region. Which host defense is most directly weakened?

options.explanation: IgA cleavage does not directly disable mitochondrial respiratory enzymes.

options.text: Chromosomal replication in every host cell
options.explanation: The protease targets antibody rather than host DNA polymerization.
Secretory IgA is not hemoglobin and its cleavage does not directly remove oxygen sites.
IgA helps prevent microbial adherence and penetration at mucosal surfaces.

explanation: Secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces partly by limiting adherence and access to epithelium. Bacterial IgA proteases can compromise this local antibody barrier. The mechanism targets immune exclusion at the mucosa rather than class switching or systemic complement pore assembly.
objective: Connect bacterial IgA proteolysis with impaired mucosal immune exclusion.
keyPoints: Connect bacterial IgA proteolysis with impaired mucosal immune exclusion.

subject: Microbiology
stem: Bacteria on a synthetic surface form a matrix-embedded community and become harder to eradicate than free-floating cells of the same strain. Which feature contributes?

options.explanation: An extracellular matrix is a defining feature of the described community.

options.text: Conversion of all bacteria into viruses
options.explanation: Surface community growth does not require a change into viral particles.

options.text: Matrix-associated community physiology and reduced susceptibility
options.explanation: Biofilms alter access, growth states, and local conditions that affect eradication.

options.text: Proof of a new resistance mutation in every organism
options.explanation: Biofilm tolerance does not require an identical new mutation in every cell.

explanation: Biofilms contain microbes embedded in an extracellular matrix with heterogeneous nutrient and growth conditions. Matrix barriers and slow-growing or persistent subpopulations can reduce susceptibility. This phenotype does not itself establish a specific inherited drug-resistance mutation.
objective: Explain biofilm persistence without assuming universal new resistance mutations.
keyPoints: Explain biofilm persistence without assuming universal new resistance mutations.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacterial population activates a virulence program only after a diffusible self-produced signal accumulates at high cell density. Which regulatory process is demonstrated?

options.explanation: The coordinated threshold response does not require random loss of chromosomes.
Accumulated signaling molecules coordinate gene expression with population density.
The response occurs within bacteria rather than host germinal-center B cells.
Density-dependent expression can occur without acquiring new genes.

explanation: Quorum sensing uses released signaling molecules whose local concentration often increases with bacterial density. Receptor-dependent detection changes gene expression across the community. The mechanism regulates an existing genetic program rather than necessarily creating a new mutation or transferring a gene.
objective: Identify density-dependent bacterial gene regulation through quorum sensing.
keyPoints: Identify density-dependent bacterial gene regulation through quorum sensing.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacterium grows in an iron-poor host environment by secreting small molecules that bind ferric iron tightly and are then recovered through specific receptors. What are these molecules?

options.explanation: Siderophores scavenge iron and support microbial acquisition of this limited nutrient.
Bacteria do not produce host immunoglobulins as their iron-scavenging system.
Cell-wall building blocks are not the characteristic secreted iron chelators.
These endocrine molecules are not the bacterial iron uptake molecules described.

explanation: Hosts restrict accessible iron as part of nutritional immunity. Bacterial siderophores bind ferric iron with high affinity, and uptake systems recover the iron-containing complexes. This supplies an essential nutrient and can contribute to virulence without directly lysing the host cell.
objective: Explain siderophore-mediated microbial acquisition of host-restricted iron.
keyPoints: Explain siderophore-mediated microbial acquisition of host-restricted iron.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A gastric bacterium hydrolyzes urea to generate ammonia near its surface. Which local effect most directly helps it persist in the acidic stomach?

options.text: Complete removal of all gastric oxygen
options.explanation: Urea hydrolysis does not require total elimination of gastric oxygen.

options.text: Direct conversion of urea into peptidoglycan
options.explanation: Urease does not directly assemble the bacterial cell wall from urea.
Urease-associated persistence does not guarantee absence of inflammation.

options.text: Buffering of the nearby acidic environment
options.explanation: Ammonia accepts protons and can raise local pH around the organism.

explanation: Urease breaks down urea, producing ammonia and carbon dioxide. Ammonia can buffer nearby hydrogen ions, supporting survival in an acidic niche. This is a local biochemical adaptation rather than complete neutralization of the entire stomach or proof that the organism is harmless.
objective: Link bacterial urease activity to local acid buffering.
keyPoints: Link bacterial urease activity to local acid buffering.

subject: Microbiology
stem: Successive isolates from a persistent mucosal infection express antigenically different pili despite originating from the same bacterial lineage. Which advantage can this provide?

options.text: Conversion of the organism into a fungus
options.explanation: Variation of a bacterial surface structure does not change its biological kingdom.

options.text: Escape from previously generated anti-pilus antibodies
options.explanation: Changing exposed antigenic sequences can reduce recognition by existing antibodies.

options.text: Permanent loss of every adhesion function
options.explanation: Antigenic variation need not abolish the ability of pili to support adherence.
Antigen changes do not automatically create universal antibiotic resistance.

explanation: Surface antigen variation can alter epitopes recognized by a previously formed antibody response. A bacterial lineage may therefore persist despite immune recognition of an earlier variant. This mechanism concerns changing antigenic identity rather than merely producing a thicker capsule or acquiring an antibiotic-resistance plasmid.
objective: Explain antibody evasion through bacterial pilus antigenic variation.
keyPoints: Explain antibody evasion through bacterial pilus antigenic variation.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacterium grows well without oxygen but poorly when exposed to air because reactive oxygen species overwhelm its defenses. Which explanation best fits its oxygen sensitivity?

options.text: Inadequate detoxification of reactive oxygen species
options.explanation: Limited protective enzymes permit oxygen-derived radicals and peroxide to accumulate.

options.text: An absolute requirement to use oxygen as final acceptor
options.explanation: Such a requirement would not explain growth only in oxygen-free conditions.
A growing bacterium necessarily retains genetic information.

options.text: Direct conversion of oxygen into its capsule
options.explanation: Capsule production does not explain the stated oxidant toxicity.

explanation: Oxygen exposure can generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide during cellular reactions. Organisms with insufficient protective systems may accumulate damaging oxidants and fail to grow in air. Anaerobic physiology is diverse, so enzyme limitations explain this stated experiment without asserting one rule for every anaerobe.
objective: Connect the stated anaerobic oxygen sensitivity with deficient oxidant detoxification.
keyPoints: Connect the stated anaerobic oxygen sensitivity with deficient oxidant detoxification.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A respiratory isolate has no peptidoglycan wall but retains a sterol-containing plasma membrane. Which structural feature explains its intrinsic insensitivity to wall-synthesis inhibitors?

options.explanation: The organism explicitly lacks this wall rather than thickening it.
The isolate remains a bacterium and does not acquire a human nucleus.

options.text: Mandatory beta-lactamase production as the only mechanism
options.explanation: No enzyme is needed when the targeted structure itself is absent.
A drug cannot block a wall-assembly process that the organism does not possess.

explanation: Mycoplasmas lack a peptidoglycan cell wall and depend on a membrane containing sterols. Wall-synthesis inhibitors therefore lack their usual target. This intrinsic structural explanation differs from an acquired enzyme that destroys a drug or a mutation in an otherwise present wall enzyme.
objective: Explain target absence as the basis of mycoplasmal wall-drug insensitivity.
keyPoints: Explain target absence as the basis of mycoplasmal wall-drug insensitivity.

subject: Microbiology
stem: An intracellular bacterium alternates between a small infectious extracellular form and a larger replicating intracellular form. Which form initiates a new chlamydial infection?

options.explanation: Chlamydiae use a distinct developmental cycle rather than a classical endospore stage.
A conidium is a fungal reproductive structure rather than a chlamydial developmental form.
The elementary body is the infectious form that enters a new host cell.
Reticulate bodies are adapted for intracellular replication rather than extracellular infection.

explanation: Chlamydial elementary bodies are adapted for transmission and entry into host cells. Inside an inclusion they differentiate into reticulate bodies that replicate, then later convert back to elementary bodies. Separating infective and replicative forms explains the biphasic developmental cycle.
objective: Identify the elementary body as the infectious chlamydial form.
keyPoints: Identify the elementary body as the infectious chlamydial form.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A rickettsial infection produces vascular leakage and widespread small-vessel inflammation. Infection of which host cell type most directly explains this vascular pathology?

options.explanation: Pigment-cell infection does not directly generate the stated systemic vasculopathy.
Rickettsial infection of vascular endothelium promotes injury and increased permeability.
Red-cell restriction would not directly account for widespread endothelial inflammation.
Pancreatic cell injury does not explain the principal small-vessel process.

explanation: Many pathogenic rickettsiae preferentially infect vascular endothelial cells. Injury and inflammatory responses disrupt barrier function, producing leakage and small-vessel pathology. This links cellular tropism to systemic manifestations rather than assuming the rash alone identifies a species.
objective: Connect rickettsial endothelial infection with vascular leakage and inflammation.
keyPoints: Connect rickettsial endothelial infection with vascular leakage and inflammation.

subject: Microbiology
stem: An inhaled bacterium survives inside alveolar macrophages by remodeling its vacuole and avoiding normal degradative trafficking. Which virulence strategy does this illustrate?

options.explanation: The organism alters its host compartment to support survival and replication.

options.text: Obligatory extracellular growth without host entry
options.explanation: The stem explicitly describes survival after macrophage uptake.
The organism does not synthesize a human antibody capsule for its vacuole.

options.text: Complete elimination of all macrophage metabolism
options.explanation: Intracellular replication depends on a usable host environment rather than total metabolic loss.

explanation: Legionella delivers bacterial effectors that remodel the phagosomal compartment into a replication-supporting niche. Avoidance of normal degradative trafficking permits intracellular survival. The mechanism differs from simply resisting phagocytosis outside the cell or killing every macrophage before replication begins.
objective: Explain Legionella survival through modification of an intracellular replication compartment.
keyPoints: Explain Legionella survival through modification of an intracellular replication compartment.

subject: Microbiology
stem: An intracellular bacterium forms an actin tail and moves into a neighboring cell through membrane protrusions. Which advantage does this Listeria strategy provide?

options.text: Avoidance of every cellular immune response
options.explanation: Intracellular spread does not make the organism invisible to all T-cell defenses.

options.text: Replacement of bacterial DNA by host actin
options.explanation: Actin provides motility rather than replacing the microbial genome.
This is active intracellular movement rather than a dormant spore transition.
Actin-driven direct spread can reduce time exposed to extracellular antibodies.

explanation: Listeria can recruit host actin polymerization to drive cytoplasmic motility and protrusion into adjacent cells. Direct spread limits exposure to extracellular immune factors while extending infection. It remains susceptible to cellular defenses, so reduced antibody exposure does not mean complete immune escape.
objective: Explain the immune-exposure advantage of actin-driven Listeria cell-to-cell spread.
keyPoints: Explain the immune-exposure advantage of actin-driven Listeria cell-to-cell spread.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacterial A-B toxin enters a host cell and ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2. Which essential cellular process is most directly impaired?

options.explanation: Lactase activity is not the direct EF-2-dependent process.
Carnitine transport does not depend directly on cytosolic EF-2 translocation.
EF-2 is needed for translocation during eukaryotic protein synthesis.
EF-2 is a translation factor rather than the enzyme sealing DNA breaks.

explanation: Diphtheria toxin transfers ADP-ribose to a modified residue on EF-2, inactivating its translation function. Ribosomal translocation fails and protein synthesis declines. The catalytic A domain therefore causes injury through a defined host target rather than through nonspecific bacterial wall inflammation.
objective: Link diphtheria toxin EF-2 modification to inhibition of protein elongation.
keyPoints: Link diphtheria toxin EF-2 modification to inhibition of protein elongation.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A bacterial toxin locks Gi proteins in an inactive state by ADP-ribosylation. Which signaling effect is expected in an appropriately responsive host cell?

options.text: Obligatory inhibition of every protein kinase
options.explanation: Increased cAMP can activate downstream signaling rather than stopping all kinases.

options.text: Reduced inhibition of adenylyl cyclase with increased cAMP
options.explanation: Inactivating Gi removes a normal inhibitory influence on cAMP production.

options.text: Permanent activation of Gi with suppressed cAMP
options.explanation: The stem specifies inactive rather than persistently active Gi.

options.text: Direct cleavage of all ribosomal RNA
options.explanation: Gi modification is distinct from toxin-mediated ribosomal damage.

explanation: Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates inhibitory G proteins and prevents normal receptor-mediated Gi activation. Loss of the inhibitory brake can increase adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP. This differs from cholera toxin, which stimulates the pathway by maintaining Gs in an active state.
objective: Distinguish Gi inactivation from Gs activation as routes to increased cAMP.
keyPoints: Distinguish Gi inactivation from Gs activation as routes to increased cAMP.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: An anthrax toxin component enters a host cell and binds calmodulin, greatly increasing cyclic AMP. What enzymatic activity does this edema factor provide?

options.explanation: Edema factor directly catalyzes cAMP generation after activation by host calmodulin.
The described product is cAMP rather than an RNA transcript.
Edema factor is not the EF-2-directed protein synthesis inhibitor.
Its principal enzymatic effect here is cyclic nucleotide production.

explanation: Anthrax edema factor is a bacterial adenylyl cyclase activated by host calmodulin after cell entry. Excess cAMP disrupts normal cellular regulation and contributes to edema. This direct enzyme delivery differs from toxins that raise cAMP by modifying host G proteins.
objective: Identify edema factor as a delivered calmodulin-dependent adenylyl cyclase.
keyPoints: Identify edema factor as a delivered calmodulin-dependent adenylyl cyclase.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: Two viruses have similar capsids, but one also requires an intact lipid envelope for entry. A lipid-disrupting detergent preferentially inactivates the enveloped virus. Why?

options.text: Detergent always selectively deletes RNA genomes
options.explanation: Lipid disruption is not universally selective for RNA rather than DNA.
All ordinary viruses retain protein components such as their capsid.

options.text: The envelope is a peptidoglycan wall
options.explanation: Viral envelopes are lipid membranes rather than bacterial cell walls.
Destroying the lipid envelope can disorganize essential attachment and fusion machinery.

explanation: An enveloped virus relies on a host-derived lipid membrane carrying viral entry proteins. Detergent disruption can destroy the organization needed for attachment or fusion. The effect follows envelope dependence rather than whether the viral genome is RNA or DNA, and susceptibility varies with conditions.
objective: Explain selective vulnerability of required viral lipid envelopes to detergent disruption.
keyPoints: Explain selective vulnerability of required viral lipid envelopes to detergent disruption.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: Purified genomic RNA from a nonretroviral positive-sense RNA virus enters a permissive cell and can direct viral protein synthesis. Why can translation begin from this RNA?

options.text: Every RNA must first integrate into a chromosome
options.explanation: Direct translation of this genome does not require chromosomal integration.

options.text: The RNA is itself a complete ribosome
options.explanation: A viral genome provides coding information rather than becoming a ribosome.

options.text: Its sequence orientation functions as messenger RNA
options.explanation: Positive-sense genomic RNA can serve directly as a ribosomal translation template.

options.text: Host ribosomes translate all negative-sense RNA directly
options.explanation: Negative-sense genomes generally require a complementary messenger RNA first.

explanation: A conventional positive-sense RNA genome has the coding orientation needed for translation. After uncoating in a suitable cell, it can direct synthesis of viral proteins, including replication machinery. New genome replication still requires additional steps, so immediate translation is not equivalent to an already complete replication cycle.
objective: Identify messenger-sense viral RNA as a direct initial translation template.
keyPoints: Identify messenger-sense viral RNA as a direct initial translation template.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A negative-sense RNA virus enters a cell. Its genome cannot be translated directly. Which enzyme must the incoming particle generally supply to begin viral messenger RNA synthesis?

options.explanation: Telomerase maintains DNA ends rather than transcribing negative-sense viral genomes.
The incoming polymerase copies negative-sense genomic RNA into translatable RNA.
DNA ligase does not transcribe an RNA genome into messenger RNA.
A digestive enzyme cannot produce viral transcripts from RNA.

explanation: Negative-sense RNA is complementary to messenger RNA and cannot directly serve as the needed translation template. Host cells lack a general RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for this task. The virion therefore packages polymerase activity to generate viral transcripts after entry.
objective: Explain why negative-sense RNA virions must carry transcriptional polymerase activity.
keyPoints: Explain why negative-sense RNA virions must carry transcriptional polymerase activity.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: An RNA virus makes a DNA copy of its genome and then inserts that copy into a host chromosome. Which viral enzyme catalyzes the chromosomal insertion step?

options.explanation: Integrase joins viral DNA ends to host chromosomal DNA during provirus formation.
Reverse transcriptase makes the DNA copy but is not the enzyme performing integration.
Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acids rather than inserting viral DNA into chromosomes.
Lactase digests lactose rather than forming a proviral integration junction.

explanation: Retroviral reverse transcription produces DNA from the RNA genome. Integrase then catalyzes insertion of this viral DNA into a host chromosome, establishing a provirus. Separating the copying and insertion steps explains why two different viral enzyme activities are required.
objective: Distinguish retroviral integrase insertion from reverse transcriptase DNA synthesis.
keyPoints: Distinguish retroviral integrase insertion from reverse transcriptase DNA synthesis.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: A DNA virus copies a pregenomic RNA intermediate back into DNA within assembling particles. Which replication feature identifies the unusual hepatitis B strategy?

options.text: Absence of all RNA during replication
options.explanation: The stated pregenomic RNA is an essential intermediate.

options.text: Mandatory integration for every new virion
options.explanation: Productive HBV replication does not require chromosomal integration each cycle.

options.text: Replication exclusively by host DNA polymerase
options.explanation: A viral reverse transcriptase performs the RNA-to-DNA copying step.
HBV uses an RNA intermediate despite carrying DNA in the infectious particle.

explanation: Hepatitis B virions carry a partially double-stranded DNA genome. Nuclear templates generate pregenomic RNA, which is reverse-transcribed during particle assembly. Genome type alone therefore does not predict that replication will use only conventional DNA-to-DNA copying.
objective: Recognize HBV DNA production through a pregenomic RNA intermediate.
keyPoints: Recognize HBV DNA production through a pregenomic RNA intermediate.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Microbiology
stem: After a mucosal herpes infection resolves, viral DNA persists in sensory neurons with limited gene expression and no continuous release of virions. Which state is described?

options.text: Permanent absence of viral genetic material
options.explanation: The genome is explicitly retained in the neuron.
Herpes persistence does not involve a bacterial spore structure.
Herpes genomes can remain as nuclear episomes and later reactivate.

options.text: Obligatory productive lysis of every neuron
